name: Hydroxycut
lead: Hydroxycut is a brand of over-the-counter weight-loss and fat-burner dietary supplements that people use during cutting and dieting phases to get leaner, with the aim of showing more muscle definition and a lower body-fat look. It was introduced in 2002 and developed by MuscleTech, a Toronto-area company whose assets were largely sold in 2003-2004 to Iovate Health Sciences, which continues to sell it. [1][2] Formulations have changed repeatedly: early versions contained ephedra, later ones included ingredients associated with liver injury, and current products are built around caffeine and plant extracts such as robusta coffee extract. [1][2]

On 1 May 2009 the US FDA warned consumers to stop using Hydroxycut products after reports of serious health problems including liver damage and at least one death, and the manufacturer issued a voluntary recall; reformulated products were later returned to market. [2] Case series in the medical literature describe liver injury associated with Hydroxycut. [3][4][5]

The company markets the products for adults combining them with diet and exercise and cites two human studies of its primary ingredient, while critics have said published evidence of effectiveness and safety for the final products is lacking. [1][2]

paras: Hydroxycut is sold as caplets, capsules, liquids and gummies, in stimulant and non-stimulant variants. [1] Current products centre on caffeine and Coffea canephora robusta extract standardised for chlorogenic acids, with variants adding yohimbe extract, apple cider vinegar, B vitamins or other botanicals; product pages describe the caffeine content of stimulant versions as comparable to about two cups of coffee. [1]

Before 2004 some formulations contained ephedra, which the FDA banned that year after 155 deaths were attributed to it, the first FDA ban of a dietary supplement. [2] Wikipedia states that pre-2009 formulations contained several substances with potential to harm the liver, including hydroxycitric acid, and that after 2009 caffeine was the only ingredient carried over. [2]
Line extensions have included Hydroxycut Hardcore, and the brand has been marketed to gym-goers as a support for diet and exercise [1][2][10].

Hydroxycut launched in 2002. MuscleTech faced ephedra-related lawsuits from 2000, with about 80 pending by 2004, and a 2003 Missouri attorney general suit over "clinically proven" fat-burner claims that settled for $100,000. [2] MuscleTech filed for bankruptcy in June 2005, and Iovate continued the brand. Xiwang Foodstuffs acquired Iovate in 2016 in a deal reported at $730 million. [2]
By 2009 about 15 percent of Americans had tried weight-loss supplements and Hydroxycut was selling around a million units a year. [2]

Hydroxycut belongs to the generation of fat burners that grew up around ephedra-caffeine stacks in bodybuilding in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Forum members on T Nation in 2009 describe having stopped fat burners when ephedra was removed from Hydroxycut, one writing that they had loved the earlier product [8], while another thread from the same year mocks supplement marketing that promises rapid results, using Hydroxycut as a joke alongside banner ads for effortless abs [9].

The manufacturer cites two human studies of its robusta coffee extract reporting average weight losses of about 10.95 pounds over 60 days and 3.7 pounds over eight weeks. [1] A 2010 paper in the World Journal of Gastroenterology criticised two studies used in Hydroxycut marketing as small, short and lacking disclosure of manufacturer funding, and noted the company had not published long-term safety or efficacy studies of its final products. [2]

The FDA's May 2009 warning cited 23 reports of serious problems including liver damage, and said liver injury appeared relatively rare. [2] A 2010 case series in the American Journal of Gastroenterology adjudicated Hydroxycut-associated liver injury after the recall, and earlier reports in the Annals of Internal Medicine (2005) and World Journal of Gastroenterology (2008) described acute hepatitis in users. [3][4][5] Broader reviews of dietary-supplement hepatotoxicity include Hydroxycut among implicated products. [6][7]

Other reports include rhabdomyolysis, a 2010 case report of atrial fibrillation linked to the green tea extract in a discontinued version, and a 2013 case report of ulcerative colitis. [2] Product labels carry caffeine warnings. [1]

Case reports describe a range of other events in users. A 37-year-old man developed recurrent sinus node arrests and a 24-second sinus pause after taking Hydroxycut Hardcore for 10 days, with symptoms resolving after he stopped [10]. A 27-year-old man with right upper quadrant pain and jaundice had a liver biopsy showing drug-induced hepatotoxicity that improved when Hydroxycut was stopped [11]. Other published case reports include hepatocellular jaundice in identical twins [12], vanishing bile duct syndrome [13], and compartment syndrome with exercise-induced rhabdomyolysis in a person taking weight-loss supplements [14]. A review of herb-induced liver injury notes that Hydroxycut is a multi-ingredient product in which it is often unclear which component is responsible, and that its hepatotoxic potential has been disputed [15].

sections.h: Use in bodybuilding and cutting communities
paras: Hydroxycut appears in bodybuilding discussions as a mainstream fat-burner brand. Users on T Nation have recalled the ephedra-era formula fondly [8], shared news stories of adverse reactions such as dizziness, stomach cramps and hallucinations reported by a woman taking it [16], and used the brand name as shorthand for over-promising supplement advertising [9].

Published clinical evidence for Hydroxycut consists of the manufacturer-cited studies of its primary ingredient and a set of case series and case reports of adverse events, mainly liver injury. [1][3][4][5] No independent randomised trial of the finished products has been identified.
Reviews of supplement-related liver injury, such as a 2015 update on herbal and dietary supplement hepatotoxicity, list weight-loss products among the implicated categories [17].

lore.intro: Hydroxycut is discussed on bodybuilding forums mostly as a nostalgic ephedra-era product or as a cautionary example of fat-burner marketing.

claims.claim: The ephedra-era Hydroxycut was the effective fat burner
claims.believers: A 2009 T Nation poster said they had not used a fat burner since ephedra was removed from Hydroxycut and that they 'loved that stuff' [8].
claims.experts: The FDA banned ephedra in 2004 after 155 deaths were attributed to it, the first ban of a dietary supplement [2].

claims.claim: Fat burners like Hydroxycut produce shredded results quickly
claims.believers: Supplement advertising of the period promised rapid leaning; a 2009 T Nation poster mocked members who believed such claims, naming Hydroxycut among them [9].
claims.experts: The maker cites two studies of its coffee extract reporting average losses of about 11 pounds over 60 days and 3.7 pounds over eight weeks; a 2010 gastroenterology paper described the two studies as small and short, with undisclosed funding [1][2].

claims.claim: Hydroxycut can cause serious side effects
claims.believers: Users have posted news stories of dizziness, severe stomach cramps, headaches and hallucinations attributed to it [16].
claims.experts: The FDA's 2009 warning cited 23 reports of serious problems including liver damage, and case series document hepatotoxicity [2][3][4][5].

card.summary: Mass-market caffeine fat burner with a 2009 FDA warning and recall after liver-injury reports; independent efficacy trials are lacking.
card.note: FDA warned consumers in 2009 and the maker recalled products; liver injury case series exist.

quick.overview:
Hydroxycut is a mainstream fat-burner brand launched in 2002 by MuscleTech and now sold by Iovate. Its formulas have changed over time, from ephedra-era versions to current caffeine and coffee-extract blends.
The company cites two studies of its coffee extract, and critics have said independent evidence for the finished products is lacking.
quick.mechanism: Current products rely mainly on caffeine, a stimulant, and robusta coffee extract (chlorogenic acids), marketed as supporting metabolism and weight loss alongside diet and exercise.
quick.risks: In 2009 the FDA warned consumers to stop using Hydroxycut products after reports of liver damage and at least one death, and the maker recalled them. Case series describe liver injury, and stimulant versions carry caffeine warnings.

chain: Caffeine and plant extracts taken alongside diet and training
Marketed as raising energy and supporting metabolism and appetite control
Support for a calorie deficit and training sessions
angle.text: People take Hydroxycut during a cut with the aim of getting leaner and more defined. The stimulant versions are used mainly for the energy and focus of caffeine around training, while the maker positions the products as aids to diet and exercise.
